918.title: Guanyin
918.hook: in China, Avalokiteshvara becomes Guanyin, the one who hears the cries of the world
918.howItsDone: Across East Asia, Buddhists call on Guanyin by name, keep her image at home and in temples, and chant the Lotus Sutra's chapter on the bodhisattva, often called the Universal Gate chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ennin's diary of the persecution of 845: bells melted, robes taken off, and a teaching that went on anyway. Your line was what survived. What old thing did you stop beside? Day nine hundred eighteen.

A white figure stands on a rock above the sea, or sits on a lotus, a small vase tipped in one hand. She is in temples and in taxi cabs, on kitchen shelves and in restaurant corners, in China and well beyond it. Fishermen have called on her in storms. Mothers have called on her at bedsides. And if you trace her back far enough, past the white robes and the vase, you arrive at an Indian bodhisattva we've already met on this path, shown in India as a man, with a long Sanskrit name. Today, how Avalokiteshvara came to be called Guanyin.
screen: `A WHITE FIGURE ABOVE THE SEA.` → `CALLED ON IN STORMS.` → `AN INDIAN NAME UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: First, the chapter. The Lotus Sutra has a chapter given over to this bodhisattva, and in China it was copied, chanted and carried on its own. In it, the Buddha is asked why the bodhisattva has this name. His answer is the heart of today. When beings in any kind of trouble call the bodhisattva's name with one mind, he perceives the sound of their voices, and they are set free. Fire, flood, shipwreck, a sword raised, chains: the chapter goes through them one by one. Second, the name. In Chinese the bodhisattva became Guanshiyin, shortened to Guanyin, and the name carries that scene inside it: the one who perceives the sounds of the world. Not the one who rules it, or the one who judges it. The one who hears. Third, the change. The same chapter says the bodhisattva takes whatever form will help the one who is suffering: a monk, a king, a child, a woman. In China, over time, Guanyin came to be pictured more and more as a woman, robed in white, gentle and near. Some Chinese stories give her a human life, like the tale of Princess Miaoshan, who gave her own eyes and arms to heal the father who had rejected her. People who love Guanyin hold both: the Indian bodhisattva of the sutra and the mother figure of the shrine. Fourth, what it asks. A bodhisattva whose whole name is listening says something about compassion. Before it fixes anything, it hears. It turns toward the sound instead of away from it. In a day full of half-heard voices, that's a small, demanding picture.
screen: `THE LOTUS SUTRA'S CHAPTER.` · `GUANYIN: PERCEIVING THE SOUNDS.` · `WHATEVER FORM WILL HELP.` · `COMPASSION STARTS BY HEARING.` · then, large: `SHE HEARS THE CRIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen fully. Settle, and let the eyes close or soften. For a minute, just listen to the sounds around you. Near ones, far ones. A hum, a voice, a car, your own breath. Don't name them or sort them into good and bad. Let each one arrive and be received. Then bring to mind one person whose voice you've only half heard lately. Picture them speaking, and in your mind, turn fully toward them. The bell holds the time.
Guanyin. The Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who perceives the sounds of the world and answers in whatever form will help. Today's word.
Your line: she hears the cries. Today, when someone talks to you, put down whatever is in your hand and hear them to the end of their sentence, and a little past it. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Korea
919.hook: a monk arrives in a Korean kingdom carrying images and texts, and the teaching takes root
919.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists remember Sundo's arrival in Goguryeo and Ichadon's death in Silla as founding moments, and Ichadon is still honored in Korea as a martyr who opened the way for the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guanyin, the bodhisattva whose name is about hearing. Your line was she hears the cries. Whose sentence did you hear all the way to the end? Day nine hundred nineteen.

A traveler arrives at a royal court on a peninsula. He is a monk, and he isn't traveling light: he brings images of the Buddha and written scriptures, sent as a gift from a Chinese ruler to a Korean king. The king could send him back. He could store the gifts in a treasury and forget them. Or he could do something that would change the country's story for a very long time. Today the road leaves China and turns east, to Korea.
screen: `A MONK FROM CHINA.` → `IMAGES AND SCRIPTURES.` → `THE ROAD TURNS EAST.`

segments.voice: First, the record. Korea was then three kingdoms: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest, Silla in the southeast. The old Korean history called the Samguk Sagi records that in 372 a Chinese ruler sent the monk Sundo to Goguryeo with images and scriptures, and that King Sosurim received him. Within a few years, the same history says, temples were built for monks to live in. Second, the welcome wasn't the same everywhere. Baekje, the history says, welcomed a foreign monk too, and the teaching spread there, and from Baekje it would later travel on across the sea. Silla, in the southeast, held out longer. Third, the hardest arrival. A Korean collection of stories called the Samguk Yusa tells of Ichadon, a young official at the Silla court. The king wanted to honor the Buddha's teaching; his nobles refused. Ichadon offered to take the blame and be put to death. The story says that when he was executed, his blood ran white like milk, and the frightened court stopped resisting. Whatever readers make of the milk, Korean Buddhist tradition remembers him as the one who opened the door in Silla. Fourth, what arrival means. A teaching doesn't land like a parcel. It comes in a monk's bag, gets a hearing at a court, meets suspicion, and slowly takes on the shape of the people who receive it. In the days ahead, Korea will give the teaching its own thinkers, its own debates, and one very large library.
screen: `SUNDO REACHES GOGURYEO.` · `THREE KINGDOMS, THREE WELCOMES.` · `ICHADON OPENS SILLA.` · `A TEACHING TAKES ROOT SLOWLY.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Korea on a map. If you have a map or a phone handy, look now; if not, picture it. Find China, and the long land road running east. Find the peninsula reaching down toward Japan. Trace with your eyes or your finger the way a monk might have walked, carrying a bundle of scriptures over mountains and rivers. Then set the map down, close your eyes, and sit with that slow road for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Korea. The peninsula where, the old histories record, a monk named Sundo arrived with images and scriptures, and the teaching took root kingdom by kingdom. Today's word.
Your line: the teaching arrives. Today, notice one thing that reached your life from far away, a food, a word, an idea, and wonder who carried it. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Wonhyo's skull
920.hook: Wonhyo drinks sweet water in the dark and in the morning sees it was in a skull: all is mind
920.carry: it was sweet in the dark
920.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists tell the story of Wonhyo's night in the tomb as a teaching on mind, and Wonhyo is honored in Korea as a great teacher and writer of commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korea: a monk with images and scriptures, a king who received him, and Ichadon in Silla. Your line was the teaching arrives. What reached you from far away? Day nine hundred twenty.

Two Korean monks, no longer young, are on the road to China, to study with the teachers there. Night falls in a storm. They find shelter in what feels like a cave and lie down, soaked and tired. In the dark, one of them, Wonhyo, wakes up desperately thirsty. He feels around, finds a vessel full of rainwater, and drinks. It's cool, and it tastes sweet. He goes back to sleep content. In the morning light he looks at what he drank from. It is a human skull, and the shelter is a tomb. His stomach turns. And then something else happens. Today, Wonhyo's skull.
screen: `A STORM ON THE ROAD TO CHINA.` → `SWEET WATER IN THE DARK.` → `MORNING: A SKULL.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Wonhyo is sick at the sight, and right in the middle of the sickness he sees it. Nothing about the water changed overnight. Last night it was sweet; this morning it's revolting. The only thing that changed was his mind. The story gives him words like these: when a thought arises, all kinds of things arise; when the thought stops, a cave and a tomb are not two. Second, the old line underneath. That isn't a new idea Wonhyo cooked up in a tomb. At Nalanda, some days back, we sat with the first verse of the Dhammapada: all that we are comes from what we have thought. And the Mahayana sutras that Wonhyo studied put it in their own words: the three realms are mind only. Wonhyo had read those words. In the tomb he tasted them. Third, how the story has been told. One early Chinese telling, in a collection of the lives of monks, has the two friends sleep in what they thought was an earthen shelter and wake to find it was an old tomb, with no skull and no water. The skull and the sweet drink come in later tellings, the version often told in Korea today. Either way, the point is the same. Fourth, the everyday version. The story suggests that much of what makes a moment sweet or foul isn't in the thing. It's in the label that gets stuck on it a second later. A message from a name you dread. A stain that turns out to be paint. The water hadn't changed. Wonhyo had.
screen: `THE WATER DIDN'T CHANGE.` · `THE THREE REALMS ARE MIND ONLY.` · `A TOMB IN THE OLDER TELLING.` · `THE LABEL COMES A SECOND LATER.` · then, large: `IT WAS SWEET IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one judgment you add. Settle, and take a few easy breaths. Now just sit, and watch what shows up: a sound, an itch, a memory, a plan. Each time something arrives, see if you can catch the tiny label that comes right after it. Annoying. Nice. Boring. Mine. You don't have to remove the label. Just notice that it came second, after the thing itself. Then let the next thing arrive. The bell holds the time.
Wonhyo's skull. The vessel he drank from in the dark: sweet at night, foul in the morning, and the same water both times. Today's word.
Your line: it was sweet in the dark. Today, when something sours the moment you see it clearly, ask what changed: the thing, or the label. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Uisang goes on
921.hook: Wonhyo turns back; his friend Uisang goes on to China and brings back Huayan
921.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists honor Uisang as the founder of Hwaeom (Huayan) in Korea, and his seal-shaped poem on the Dharma realm is still recited and studied in Korean temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wonhyo's skull: the same water, sweet at night and foul in the morning. Your line was it was sweet in the dark. Which label did you catch arriving a second late? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Morning, outside the tomb. Two friends stand on the road with their bundles. One of them has just had the night of his life. Wonhyo says he doesn't need to go to China anymore: if the mind makes everything, there's nothing over there he can't find right here. He turns around and walks home. The other friend, Uisang, listens, and nods, and picks up his bundle. He keeps walking toward the sea. No quarrel in the story. No one is called wrong. Today, the friend who went on.
screen: `ONE TURNS BACK.` → `ONE PICKS UP HIS BUNDLE.` → `NO QUARREL.`

segments.voice: First, where Uisang went. He crossed to China and studied with the teacher Zhiyan, in the school called Huayan, which takes its name from the Flower Garland Sutra. We met that school's name on the list of Chinese schools. Second, what he brought back. Huayan pictures the universe as a net of jewels, where every jewel reflects every other one. Nothing stands alone; each thing holds the whole. Uisang packed that teaching into a short poem, written in a winding pattern like a seal, so the reader's eye follows a path that folds back on itself. One of its lines says, in plain terms, in one is all, and in many is one. Back in Korea, Uisang founded temples and taught students, and Huayan, called Hwaeom in Korean, took root. Third, a story along the way. An old Chinese life of Uisang tells of Shanmiao, Seonmyo in Korean, a young woman in China who loved him. When he sailed home, she threw herself into the sea and became a dragon to guard his ship, and later a great rock to protect his temple. Fourth, Wonhyo's road. He never went to China. He stayed, wrote commentaries, and later, the stories say, left the monk's life to walk among villagers, singing and teaching them the Buddha's name. One friend took the long road out; one took the short road in. Korean Buddhist tradition honors both. And there's an echo of Huayan in that: two very different paths, each holding something of the other.
screen: `UISANG STUDIES HUAYAN IN CHINA.` · `A NET OF JEWELS, A SEAL-SHAPED POEM.` · `SEONMYO GUARDS HIS SHIP.` · `WONHYO SINGS IN THE VILLAGES.` · then, large: `TWO FRIENDS, TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a friend's different path. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a friend, a sibling, someone you started out beside, who went a different way from you. A different city, a different kind of work, a different pace. Picture them on their road and you on yours. Notice any urge to call one of the roads the right one, and let it rest. Wish them well on their path, the way Uisang and Wonhyo parted without a quarrel. The bell holds the time.
Huayan. The school Uisang studied in China and carried home to Korea: a universe where every jewel reflects every other jewel. Today's word.
Your line: two friends, two paths. Today, send one short message to someone whose road went another way, and ask how their road is going. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Sudden and gradual
922.hook: Chinul: awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually
922.howItsDone: In Korean Seon, Chinul's teaching of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation is studied in monasteries, and his short works, such as Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, are read by monks and lay practitioners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uisang brought home Huayan: one friend to China, one friend home, and no quarrel. Your line was two friends, two paths. Whose road did you ask about? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A frozen pond in winter. Anyone who walks up to it knows, in one glance, that the whole thing is water. Not partly water. All of it. And yet you still can't drink it, or swim in it, or wash your hands in it. Knowing it's water doesn't melt it. That takes days of sun. A Korean monk named Chinul used that pond to answer an argument that had run through Chan for a long time, the one we met at the wall where two verses were written. Today, Buddha-nature.
screen: `A FROZEN POND.` → `ALL OF IT IS WATER.` → `KNOWING DOESN'T MELT IT.`

segments.voice: First, the old argument. Some days back, two verses went up on a monastery wall. One said the mind is a mirror that must be wiped clean, again and again. Huineng's answer said there is no mirror for dust to land on. People came to sum up the two sides as gradual and sudden: is awakening built up step by step, or is it seen all at once? Second, Chinul's answer. Chinul was a Korean monk of the Goryeo kingdom who trained and taught in Korea. In a short work called Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, he says: both, in order. First you awaken suddenly. You see, all at once, that your own mind is already the Buddha-nature, the way you see that ice is water. Then you cultivate gradually. Old habits are still frozen in place, and they take time and steady practice to thaw. Third, his other picture. A newborn baby, Chinul writes, has all the senses and limbs of a grown person, nothing missing. But it takes years before that strength is fully grown. Awakening is like being born. Practice is like growing up. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Insight has a way of arriving in a flash: in a conversation, on a walk, at a funeral. The temptation is to think the flash is the finish. Chinul says the flash is the start. The seeing is real. The thaw still has to happen. Korean Seon, Korea's Chan, still looks back to Chinul as one of its great teachers.
screen: `THE MIRROR AND NO MIRROR.` · `FIRST AWAKEN, THEN CULTIVATE.` · `A NEWBORN STILL HAS TO GROW.` · `THE FLASH IS THE START.` · then, large: `SUDDEN, THEN SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep practicing after an insight. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one thing you've understood clearly at some point, about yourself, or someone you love, or how you want to live. Something you saw in a flash. Now, gently, ask where the ice is still frozen: where the old habit still runs, even though you know better. Don't scold it. Just sit beside it, like sun on a pond, for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Buddha-nature. The true mind Chinul says you see all at once, then thaw slowly through steady practice. Today's word.
Your line: sudden, then slowly. Today, take one thing you already know you want to change, and give it a small, slow step: five minutes, one call, one honest sentence. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

pairs: nothing missing, still has to grow

923.title: Eighty thousand woodblocks
923.hook: after invaders burn the first set, Korea carves the whole canon again in wood: the Tripitaka Koreana
923.howItsDone: The Tripitaka Koreana is kept at Haeinsa temple in Korea, where monks care for the blocks, and visitors come to see the halls that hold them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha-nature: the ice is all water, and it still has to thaw. Your line was sudden, then slowly. What slow step did you take? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

A carver bends over a block of wood. On it, written backward so it will print the right way round, are the characters of a Buddhist scripture. He cuts away everything that isn't a letter. One slip of the knife and a word is gone. Around him, more blocks wait, and more after those, enough to fill a library. This is Korea under the Goryeo kings, and the reason for all this patient cutting is a fire. Today, Tripitaka Koreana.
screen: `A CARVER, A KNIFE, A BLOCK.` → `LETTERS CUT BACKWARD.` → `THE REASON IS A FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the fire. Goryeo had already carved the Buddhist canon once, the Tripitaka, the three baskets of teaching. Then Mongol armies invaded, and that first set of blocks was burned. Second, the answer. The court and the monks decided to carve the whole canon again. A prayer written for the work by the scholar Yi Gyubo asks the Buddhas and protectors to look on the effort and turn the invaders back. So the carving was scholarship and devotion at once: every block a page of scripture, and the whole a vow. Third, the care. The texts were compared and corrected against other editions before the cutting began. Tradition says the carvers bowed after each character. In Korea the collection is known as the Palman Daejanggyeong, the Eighty Thousand Tripitaka, after its blocks. Today they are kept at Haeinsa, a temple in the mountains, in long wooden halls built with slatted windows to let the air move through. Fourth, why it lasts. A burned set taught them that words can be lost. Their answer wasn't despair, and it wasn't speed. It was slowness, done right. Some things are made to be used up today. Others are made to outlast the people who made them. The carvers of Goryeo chose the second kind, one letter at a time.
screen: `THE FIRST SET BURNED.` · `CARVED AGAIN AS A VOW.` · `A BOW, TRADITION SAYS, FOR EACH CHARACTER.` · `KEPT AT HAEINSA.` · then, large: `CARVED TO LAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one careful line. If you have paper and a pen, take them now; if not, trace the letters with a finger on your palm or your knee. Choose one line that matters to you: a line from this path, a name, a sentence you want to keep. Write it as slowly as you can, one letter at a time, as if it had to last a long time. When it's done, put the pen down and sit with the line in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Tripitaka Koreana. The Buddhist canon carved again in wood after invaders burned the first set, and kept at Haeinsa. Today's word.
Your line: carved to last. Today, do one small thing the slow, careful way, a meal, a note, a repair, as if someone years from now might find it. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.title: Japan
924.hook: a Korean king sends a bronze Buddha across the sea; a divided court, and then Prince Shotoku
924.howItsDone: Japanese Buddhists honor Prince Shotoku as an early patron of the teaching, and temples linked to him, such as Horyuji near Nara, are still places of worship and pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tripitaka Koreana, the canon carved again after the fire. Your line was carved to last. What did you do the slow, careful way? Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A ship crosses the strait from Korea. On board, wrapped for the journey, is a Buddha made of gilt bronze, with banners, canopies and rolls of scripture. It's a gift from the king of Baekje, one of the Korean kingdoms we met a few days ago, to the ruler of Japan. With it comes a letter praising the teaching as hard to grasp and wonderful beyond measure. The ruler of Japan opens the gift, looks at the shining face, and does what rulers do with something new and powerful. He asks his ministers. Today the road crosses the sea, to Japan.
screen: `A GILT BRONZE BUDDHA.` → `A GIFT FROM BAEKJE.` → `THE RULER ASKS HIS MINISTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the gift. Japan's old chronicle, the Nihon Shoki, tells this story in the reign of Emperor Kinmei. The image and scriptures came from Baekje, so the teaching reached Japan by way of Korea. Second, the divided court. The chronicle says the ministers split. The Soga clan said the neighbors honor this Buddha, so should we. The Mononobe and Nakatomi clans said the land's own gods would be angered. Kinmei handed the image to the Soga chief to honor at his house, as a trial. Then sickness swept the country, the opponents blamed the foreign Buddha, and the image was thrown into a canal. The arrival was not smooth. Third, Prince Shotoku. Later, the chronicle tells of a regent, Prince Shotoku, who studied the sutras with teachers from Korea and gave the teaching a home at court. The chronicle credits him with a set of seventeen guiding articles for officials. The first asks for harmony. The second asks that the three treasures be sincerely revered: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. Tradition links him to the founding of temples, among them Horyuji, near Nara. Japanese Buddhists honor him as a founding patron. Fourth, the week that brought us here. Guanyin hearing the cries in China. Korea receiving a monk with scriptures. Wonhyo's sweet water. Uisang walking on. Chinul's frozen pond. The woodblocks. And now a bronze Buddha crossing the sea. Again and again this week, the teaching arrived from somewhere else, met doubt or hardship, and found people to carry it.
screen: `A GIFT FROM BAEKJE.` · `A COURT DIVIDED.` · `SHOTOKU REVERES THE THREE TREASURES.` · `A WEEK OF ARRIVALS.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Nara on a map. A phone, an atlas or your memory will do. This time, start from the water: the strait between the Korean peninsula and the islands of Japan. Follow a ship across it, then go inland to Nara, among low hills, where tomorrow's story waits. Rest your eyes there for a moment. Then let the map go, and sit with the picture of one small boat, its shining cargo, and the water moving under it. The bell holds the time.
Japan. Where, the old chronicle says, a gilt bronze Buddha arrived as a gift from Korea, a court argued over it, and Prince Shotoku asked that the three treasures be revered. Today's word.
Your line: the teaching arrives. Today, when something new comes your way, notice the first doubt and give the new thing a fair hearing anyway. That's the week. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

fork.setup: you're the emperor. a gilt bronze Buddha has arrived from Korea, and your ministers disagree about it. what do you do?
options: throw it into the sea at once.
hand it to the clan that favors it, as a trial.
make it the court's only worship.
